title: ASIRT handed Grande Prairie RCMP in-custody death investigation after outcry from family
article: An investigation into the death of a Grande Prairie man at the local RCMP detachment will now be handled by the province's independent police watchdog - not Mounties themselves - after criticism from the man's family.

Addison Hartzler, 30, died June 3 after being found unresponsive in a cell nine hours after his arrest for mischief. Gregory Hartzler claims RCMP committed "gross negligence" by failing to medically assess his son and check on him at least every 15 minutes while he was in the cell.

Initially, Alberta government officials told Hartzler the RCMP would investigate whether its officers played a role in Addison's death, citing workload issues with the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT), the arm's-length agency that probes serious cases of police misconduct.

But after family issued a press release Wednesday criticizing the move , an ASIRT official called to say the investigation had been transferred. Officials with both ASIRT and the RCMP confirmed the change in agency Thursday, saying the file was handed to ASIRT Aug. 9 and that the family wasn't informed prior to the news release.
Neither RCMP nor the Alberta government responded to requests for comment Wednesday.

Addison Hartzler was one of two men to die in Grande Prairie RCMP custody in the span of a year-and-a-half. Family said he was arrested after calling 911 about a break-in at his home. Police told them no evidence of a break-in was found, and that Addison was arrested for making a false report. He was allegedly "psychotic and delusional" and refused to give his name, leading police to lodge him in cells.

Gregory Hartzler said that to his knowledge, his son had no mental health issues and was not an active substance user. An autopsy deemed his cause of death "inconclusive" pending additional blood and tissue analysis. An EMS report said Addison was "obviously dead" by the time paramedics arrived.

Gregory Hartzler said the province's director of law enforcement, who decides how to handle serious police misconduct cases, initially said the investigation would remain with RCMP because there was no "confrontation" between RCMP and Addison prior to his death, and because of the number of files recently assigned to ASIRT.

In a statement Thursday, Alberta Justice spokesman Jason van Rassel said the director, Marlin Degrand, raised the issue "in the interest of being fully transparent regarding the capacity challenges the agency was facing."

"ASIRT's resourcing issues at the time were well-known," van Rassel said in an email. "However, when deciding which agency will investigate a death in custody, the overriding consideration is always to ensure that the case is fully and properly investigated and to maintain public confidence."
No timeline has been set for the investigation.
